problem: Prior latent-state discovery methods (autoencoders, contrastive, forward generative, one-step inverse models, Ex-BMDP PPE) either capture exogenous noise, need resets or deterministic initial states, or need a given factorized encoder; one-step inverse models provably merge distinct states.
motivation: Agents receive high-dimensional observations dominated by irrelevant, temporally correlated distractors. A minimal state that is sufficient for control would give better exploration, planning and interpretability. Multi-step action prediction plus a bottleneck could give a provable and practical way to obtain it without rewards.
key_idea: Train an encoder with a multi-step inverse model (predict the first action from the current and a k-step-future observation) under a discrete VQ plus Gaussian information bottleneck, so only the minimal control-endogenous state is kept.
insight: Theory shows the Bayes-optimal multi-step inverse model depends only on the endogenous state under an endogenous policy, and that the endogenous partition is the coarsest partition consistent with it, whereas one-step inverse models have a counterexample where distinct states merge. On the real robot arm, 1-step inverse gets 86.75% ground-truth state accuracy against 99.83% for AC-State. The bottleneck is essential, since otherwise the identity encoder is optimal.
method: Multi-step inverse objective: predict the first action a_t from f(x_t) and f(x_{t+k}), with k sampled uniformly from 1..K, using a log-loss.
Information bottleneck: a Gaussian variational bottleneck followed by VQ-VAE vector quantization gives a discrete minimal latent, added as loss terms on x_t and x_{t+k}.
Random-policy variant: data collected with a uniform random (trivially endogenous) policy; the encoder is trained on it.

Planning-policy variant: a count-based tabular MDP is built over learned discrete states; MC BFS picks rarely seen goals, Dijkstra plans to them, and only the first random action of each goal-seeking trajectory is predicted.
Evaluation: latent transition counts estimate T(s'|s,a); a dynamics-difference L1 error and a parsimony ratio (ground-truth states / discovered states) are measured against ground truth.
Theory: deterministic Ex-BMDP, Bayes-optimality proof, coarsest-partition induction proof over the horizon, and an episodic finite-sample bound.

setting.backbone: MLP-Mixer/FFN encoder + VQ-VAE (maze); CNN (robot arm); ViT 6-layer, 256-d + VQ-VAE (Matterport), trained from scratch
setting.training_data: Self-collected reward-free random-policy or planned-exploration data: 14,000 real robot arm samples (6 h), 3,000-25,000 maze samples, one 20,000-transition Matterport episode
setting.observation: Raw images (robot 256x256 front camera; maze 80x720x3; Matterport 12-view panorama)
setting.action_space: Discrete high-level actions (robot arm 5 moves; maze 4 moves + 4 reset actions; Matterport neighbouring viewpoint)
setting.simulator: Matterport3D simulator, custom multi-maze gridworld, real AR3 robot arm
setting.privileged: none (ground-truth states used only for evaluation)

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark; Matterport results are only in a figure (values not in text). Other experiments (maze, robot arm) are custom, not canonical benchmarks.
results: On the 4-room reset maze with 25,000 samples, AC-State explores 68/68 true states with 0.00% dynamics error, versus Contrastive 20/68 (92.2%), Autoencoder 20/68 (91.7%) and Forward Generative 25/68 (97.1%). On the real robot arm it reaches 99.83% ground-truth state accuracy and 0.52% dynamics error, against 86.75% and 16.6% for the 1-step inverse. On Matterport it has the highest accuracy and parsimony in a figure.
limitations: Requires discrete finite endogenous state, deterministic endogenous dynamics, bounded diameter, and a high-coverage endogenous data policy.
Needs more codes than true states and depends on the discrete bottleneck.
Evaluated only on small or toy settings with no downstream task or navigation benchmark performance; theory is asymptotic.
